cable: 2 AWG fine-strand, loomed, grommeted, pull string beside it in the tunnel
protection: Class-T 150 A at the battery — the PMU stud's maximum
why: Class-T is the only common fuse with the interrupt rating to break a lithium short. The cable between post and fuse is the one length that can never be protected — keep it inches long. The master disconnect is no longer in this leg (D-245)
Cranking pulls 300–500 A briefly and cannot pass through the 150 A Class-T. 1/0 over 18 ft keeps about half a volt at the starter that 2 AWG would have lost (D-246)

protection: F18 100 A MIDI at the stud
why: The alternator charges through the starter cable, as the factory did through its fusible link

protection: F17 30 A MIDI at the stud
why: The start relay's contact current never touches the PMU; O21 only drives the coil

run: Battery − → master disconnect → rear ground stud
why: The disconnect lives here (D-245). Open it and every positive fault in the car loses its return — the starter cable included — so the switch means what the design always claimed. Bare metal, star washer, cavity wax at the stud

run: Rear ground stud → engine block (through the tunnel)
cable: 1/0, loomed, pulled beside the starter feed
why: The dedicated cranking return (D-246). Without it 400 A crosses the whole unibody through 44-year-old spot welds and seam sealer; the factory never asked the shell to do this because the battery was in the engine bay. B6 stays as the block-to-chassis bond, not the main return
The cranking return. Without it the current finds its own path through throttle cables and sender wires
